rationale: A wins because its kept angles mostly survive on the supplied facts: ownership model, public-company economics, materials, and reverse logistics are four real doors into the story. Its best line, "The hard part of a circular sneaker is the mail," finds the operational fight hiding inside the announcement. B has the sharpest single skeptical frame, "It hasn't said how much of the loop closes," but then keeps "What it's actually like to rent your running shoes" and starts borrowing a named customer story it has not earned.
gaps_in_A: "commercial-scale test for castor-bean materials" overstates what the update proves; nationwide launch does not disclose production volume or material scale.
"take-back programs are widely seen as the operational graveyard of circular retail" imports an unsourced industry claim. Useful tension, but it needs proof or softer framing.
It buries the strongest skeptical sustainability story in proof needs. "recycling-rate and per-unit economics are not disclosed" deserved its own claim-verification angle.
"commercial deployment" is a little too confident for a subscription rollout with no subscriber count, return rate, or recycling rate disclosed.
gaps_in_B: "people who have already done a full cycle" is invented from "limited pilot." A pilot does not automatically give you named runners who completed run-return-replace.
"What it's actually like to rent your running shoes" should be conditional or refused until a named pilot subscriber exists. Otherwise it is a service piece made out of hope.
"mandatory return" overstates the mechanics. The update says subscribers mail shoes back; it does not state penalties, cadence, or enforcement.
It misses the standalone reverse-logistics story. The mail-back, grinding, remaking loop is not just consumer experience or sustainability claims; it is a supply-chain beat.
